Methods for the Expectation of a Derivative

Source: R/expected_derivatives.R
expected_derivative_methods.Rd

An expected derivative of the log-density, such as the expected Hessian (the negative of the Fisher information) or the expected third derivative, is the expectation \(\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\,]\) of a function of the response taken under the distribution at the parameters. A family may write that expectation in closed form. When it does not, or when a different route is wanted, the expectation is obtained by one of three methods, which are objects: expect_opg(), expect_integrate() and expect_mc(). All of them inherit from ExpectMethod and are passed through the argument method of distrib_expected_hessian(), distrib_deriv3(), distrib_deriv4(), the derivatives of the expected information (distrib_dexpected_hessian() and the functions of its family), fisher_scoring() and expected_info().

The argument method has one rule. If it is NULL, which is the default, the function returns the closed form of the family where the family has one, and otherwise the default route of that function (the table below). If it is an object, the object is always used, also for a family that has the expectation in closed form; the closed form is then bypassed, and the result is the expectation as the method computes it.

Value

Nothing. This page documents the argument method shared by the functions named above; the value returned is theirs.

Two identities and three ways

Let \(\ell\) be the log-density and \(\ell_{i}, \ell_{ij}, \dots\) its derivatives with respect to the parameters. The expected derivative of order \(k\) has two expressions inside the expectation, which are equal in expectation for a regular model.

The Hessian identity

The expectation of the observed derivative of order \(k\) itself, $$\mathbb{E}[\ell_{i_1 \dots i_k}].$$ At order 2 this is the expected Hessian read literally.

The score identity

The Bartlett partition identity, which writes the same expectation through products of derivatives of lower order. The identity states that $$\sum_{\pi} \mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{B \in \pi} \ell_B\right] = 0,$$ where \(\pi\) runs over the partitions of the index set \(\{i_1,\dots,i_k\}\) and \(\ell_B\) is the derivative with respect to the parameters indexed by the block \(B\). The single-block partition is the target, so that $$\mathbb{E}[\ell_{i_1 \dots i_k}] = -\sum_{\pi,\ |\pi| \ge 2} \mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{B \in \pi} \ell_B\right].$$ At order 2 this is \(-\mathbb{E}[\ell_i \ell_j]\), at order 3 \(-\mathbb{E}[\ell_{ij}\ell_k + \ell_{ik}\ell_j + \ell_{jk}\ell_i + \ell_i\ell_j\ell_k]\), and at order 4 the sum over the partitions of four indices into at least two blocks. The target order is never needed.

The expectation of either quantity is then obtained in one of three ways: computed by quadrature (or by a series over the support of a discrete family), simulated, or estimated from the sample in hand. The methods fill the table as follows.

computed by quadraturesimulatedestimated from the sample
Hessian identityexpect_integrate(identity = "hessian")expect_mc(identity = "hessian")not available
score identityexpect_integrate(identity = "score")expect_mc(identity = "score")expect_opg()

The estimate from the sample has no Hessian-identity entry because the observed derivative at the data, averaged over the observations, is the observed information and not an expectation. Reading the score identity at the data gives the empirical outer product of the scores, which is the BHHH estimator at order 2.

expect_integrate()

Computes the expectation by batched adaptive quadrature for a continuous family and by series summation for a discrete one. It is deterministic, and it is normally the most accurate method. With identity = "hessian" it costs one integral per component and needs the derivative of the target order, which every family of the package supplies or approximates by finite differences. With identity = "score" it costs one integral per partition and component and needs only the lower orders, which is the reason to choose it where only those are available in closed form. The tolerances and limits are arguments of the constructor. For a family with several parameters varying by observation, one integral is computed per distinct parameter configuration.

expect_mc()

Draws nsim observations from the distribution, with distrib_rng(), at each parameter configuration and averages the quantity of the identity over them. It estimates the same quantity as expect_integrate() with the same identity. The error decreases as \(1/\sqrt{n_{sim}}\), and the result is reproducible only if the seed is fixed. The cost is that of distrib_rng() times nsim, per parameter configuration. It is the simplest method where quadrature performs poorly (heavy tails, awkward supports); for a distribution whose generator inverts a slow quantile function, expect_integrate() is cheaper.

expect_opg()

Reads the score identity at each observation and takes no expectation: nothing is integrated and nothing is simulated. At order 2 the quantity is \(-\ell_i \ell_j\), evaluated with one call to distrib_gradient(); at orders 3 and 4 it is the sum of products of the identity, evaluated with the derivatives of orders 1 to \(k-1\). Each observation contributes a noisy rank-one-like term, and the sum over \(n\) observations converges to \(n\) times the expectation at the rate \(n^{-1/2}\). At order 2 the matrix is positive semidefinite by construction, which makes it adequate for the step of Fisher scoring, and it has the same fixed point as the expected information. The variance grows with the order, because the terms are products of up to \(k\) derivatives. The method is never routed to quadrature at any order.

Defaults of each function

When method is NULL, the function returns the closed form of the family where there is one. The route used otherwise is:

distrib_expected_hessian()expect_opg()
distrib_deriv3() and distrib_deriv4() with expected = TRUEexpect_integrate() (identity = "hessian")
fisher_scoring() and expected_info()expect_opg() (order 2)
distrib_dexpected_hessian(), distrib_d2expected_hessian(), distrib_d3expected_hessian() and distrib_d4expected_hessian()none: a family without a closed form signals an error

These defaults reproduce the values that the functions returned before method was introduced.

Derivatives of the expected information

The functions that return the derivatives of the expected information with respect to the parameters have the closed form of the family as their only default. With a method, the \(m\)th derivative of the matrix \(E_{ab}(\theta)\) that the method defines is returned.

For expect_integrate() and expect_mc() the matrix is the expectation \(E_{ab}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\theta[f_{ab}]\) of the integrand \(f_{ab}\) of the identity (\(\ell_{ab}\) for the Hessian identity and \(-\ell_a\ell_b\) for the score identity), and the derivative moves the density as well as the integrand, $$\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_c}\mathbb{E}_\theta[f] = \mathbb{E}_\theta\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_c} + f\,\ell_c\right],$$ repeated for higher orders. The expectation of the right-hand side is taken by the method.

For expect_opg() the matrix is the sum over the observations of \(-\ell_a\ell_b\) at the data, which is the matrix whose inverse the scoring step uses, and the density does not move: the exact derivative of that matrix with respect to \(\theta_c\) is, per observation, $$-\left(\ell_{ac}\,\ell_b + \ell_a\,\ell_{bc}\right),$$ and the second derivative is $$-\left(\ell_{acd}\,\ell_b + \ell_{ac}\,\ell_{bd} + \ell_{ad}\,\ell_{bc} + \ell_a\,\ell_{bcd}\right).$$ These are not estimates of \(\partial \mathbb{E}[\ell_{ab}]/\partial \theta_c\), which contains the moved density; they are the derivatives of the matrix that expect_opg() returns, and a criterion built on that matrix needs these. The derivatives of order 3 and 4 follow the same rule by Leibniz's formula.

A derivative of order \(m\) of the matrix needs the observed derivatives of the log-density up to order \(m+1\) for the score identity, which is always the case for \(m \le 4\), and up to order \(m+2\) for the Hessian identity, which is available for \(m \le 3\); for \(m = 4\) the Hessian identity signals an error that names identity = "score".

A kink in the log-density

Where the log-density has a kink in a parameter, the observed second derivative has a point mass at the kink, and an average of its pointwise values does not contain that mass. For the Laplace location, \(\ell_{\mu\mu}\) is zero almost everywhere, so its pointwise average is zero, while the information is \(1/\sigma^2\). The information of such a family is the variance of the score, which the score identity evaluates. For a family that declares a non-smooth parameter (see param_smoothness()), the Hessian identity at order 2, whether by expect_integrate() or by expect_mc(), signals an error that names identity = "score". expect_opg(), which uses the score identity, and identity = "score" remain valid. When the family declares where its kink is, through kink_decomposition(), the quadrature of expectation() places a knot there.

See also

expect_opg(), expect_integrate() and expect_mc() for the constructors; ExpectMethod for the classes; distrib_expected_hessian(), distrib_deriv3() and distrib_deriv4(), the generics that take method; distrib_dexpected_hessian() for the derivatives of the expected information; fisher_scoring(), where it is set for a fit; expected_info() and observed_info(), the objects that select the information of a fit, and information_objects for their comparison; expected_by_bartlett(), expected_by_integrate() and expected_by_mc() for the implementations.

Examples

# A family defined by its density alone has no closed-form information.
Dens <- S7::new_class("Dens", parent = continuous_distrib)
S7::method(distrib_pdf, Dens) <- function(distrib, y, theta, log = FALSE, ...) {
  stats::dnorm(y, theta[[1]], theta[[2]], log = log)
}
d <- Dens(distrib_name = "dens", dimension = "univariate",
          bounds = c(-Inf, Inf), params = c("mu", "sigma"),
          params_interpretation = c(mu = "location", sigma = "scale"),
          n_params = 2L,
          params_bounds = list(mu = c(-Inf, Inf), sigma = c(0, Inf)),
          link_params = list(mu = linkfunctions7::identity_link(),
                             sigma = linkfunctions7::log_link()),
          params_smooth = c(mu = TRUE, sigma = TRUE))
th <- list(mu = 0, sigma = 2)
y <- c(-1, 0.5, 2)

# The sigma-sigma entry of the expected Hessian is -2 / sigma^2 = -0.5.
# The two quadratures agree; the empirical outer product of the scores is
# the value at one observation, and Monte Carlo carries sampling error.
methods <- list(
  opg = expect_opg(),
  integrate_hessian = expect_integrate(identity = "hessian"),
  integrate_score = expect_integrate(identity = "score"),
  mc_hessian = expect_mc(nsim = 2000, identity = "hessian"),
  mc_score = expect_mc(nsim = 2000, identity = "score")
)
set.seed(3)
vapply(methods, function(m) {
  distrib_expected_hessian(d, y, th, method = m)$sigma_sigma[1]
}, numeric(1))
#>               opg integrate_hessian   integrate_score        mc_hessian 
#>        -0.1406250        -0.5000000        -0.5000000        -0.4575573 
#>          mc_score 
#>        -0.4840274 

# An object is used also by a family that has a closed form.
g <- gaussian1_distrib()
distrib_expected_hessian(g, 0, list(mu = 0, sigma = 2))$sigma_sigma
#> [1] -0.5
distrib_expected_hessian(g, 0, list(mu = 0, sigma = 2),
                         method = expect_integrate())$sigma_sigma
#> [1] -0.5
